national.title: As Americans drown in medical debt, how one family found a lifeline
national.summary: Coy and Caty Smith are gainfully employed and have health insurance. But when illness struck, the bills piled up fast — here's how they found their way back to financial health.
national.body: Coy Smith and his wife were getting up to 16 phone calls a day, all to discuss the same topic — how they planned to pay off the thousands of dollars in medical bills their family had racked up after facing a series of serious healthcare issues. By 2023, the family was more than $30,000 in the hole, including credit card debt they had taken on to help pay their medical bills."It's very stressful knowing that every time the phone rings, you have to pick it up and talk to someone who says you owe them thousands of dollars for something you couldn't help," Coy, 32, a Cypress, Texas, resident, told CBS News. 40% of AmericansThe phone is also ringing off the hook for millions of other people facing overdue healthcare bills. Roughly 40% of Americans are saddled with debt for medical care not covered by insurance, treatment for complex medical conditions, and hospitalization costs for serious injuries or illnesses, according to health policy and research firm KFF.Those debts are often financially debilitating, with high healthcare costs topping the list of financial worries for U.S. voters, a recent KFF poll shows. To stay on top of their medical bills, people may cut spending on essentials like food, exhaust emergency savings and tap their retirement funds."There's no other way to state it than as a parent and American, you dread having to go to the doctor and having to go to the hospital," Smith said. "You know it's going to cost thousands of dollars just to walk in the door."Smith also said he was routinely advised to take out a personal loan to consolidate the family's crushing debt. But that approach carried its own financial risks. national.title: Bigger and more-frequent wildfires threaten water supplies across the U.S.
national.summary: Wildfires leave behind charred trees and scorched vegetation that impact the streams and rivers providing drinking water to much of the country, and new studies show that contamination could remain for more than a decade.
national.body:
Martha Bellisle, Associated Press Martha Bellisle, Associated Press

Wildfires leave behind charred trees and scorched vegetation that impact the streams and rivers providing drinking water to much of the country, and new studies show that contamination could remain for more than a decade.

These findings about the longevity of contamination in the nation's drinking water supplies are especially concerning as climate change and increasingly strong El Niño weather events, which intensify drought conditions, have led to bigger and more frequent wildfires in the U.S. So far in 2026, there have been 68,179 blazes burning more than 14,062 square miles (36,420 square kilometers).

After a wildfire sweeps through hillsides and forests, rains carry ash and organic matter into the streams that feed water treatment plants for towns and cities alike. Communities are working to adapt, but it can take years and require stopgap solutions.

People in the City of Las Vegas, New Mexico, went without water for months after the Hermit's Peak/Calf Canyon wildfire contaminated the Gallinas River in 2022. In the four years since, they've had to give residents bottled water and ship tanks in from nearby towns as they collected funds to build a new treatment plant.

WATCH: How a super El Niño is fueling extreme weather patterns

Karen Pettine, who has owned the Hillcrest Restaurant for 50 years, said the water crisis forced them to close, sometimes for a week at a time.

"It's hard to run a restaurant without good water," she said. "We used some paper plates at times. They brought in semi-truckloads of bottled water. You could pick up four cases at a time. The water situation is ongoing because when it rains, it floods and it brings dirty water down the stream."

national.title: Criminal probe launched into cruise ship over potential "magic pipe"
national.summary: The U.S. Coast Guard launched an investigation into a so-called "magic pipe" case, in which a ship transfers its oil discharge into its gray water system.
national.body: The MSC Poesia cruise ship, which was cleared to depart the Port of Miami on Thursday after being detained earlier this month, is under investigation for allegedly discharging oil illegally at sea, according to a U.S. official familiar with the probe.The U.S. Coast Guard launched the criminal investigation into a so-called "magic pipe" case, in which a ship transfers its oil discharge into its gray water system. This is illegal under federal law.Gray water — which includes anything from a sink or shower — can be discharged at sea as long as the ship is a safe distance from the shore.The investigation could target crew members, the owner of the vessel, and whoever may have been directly involved and therefore potentially criminally liable, according to the U.S. official. CBS News has reached out to MSC Cruises, which operates the ship, for comment.The MSC Poesia was detained at the Port of Miami earlier this month after the U.S. Coast Guard, which has jurisdiction to inspect foreign-flagged vessels entering U.S. ports, "identified deficiencies with systems on board the vessel." At the time, MSC Cruises described the issue as a "regulatory matter" and no further details were provided.More than 2,000 people were on board the MSC Poesia at the time of its detention, a source familiar with the matter told CBS News.Using a so-called "magic pipe" could lead to hefty fines. In 2016, Carnival's Princess Cruises was ordered to pay a $40 million fine for dumping oily waste into the ocean. It was the largest penalty of its kind at the time. The company also pleaded guilty to seven felony charges.

Alice Huang flew into Singapore in June 2025 for a voluntary interview with Singapore-based investigators from the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security, according to the source. national.title: Bessent blames Lutnick's Commerce Department for not restricting Nvidia chips to China
national.summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has come under increasing scrutiny because of his reportedly close relationship with Jensen Huang.
national.body:
Mike Catalini, Associated Press Mike Catalini, Associated Press

Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday he was frustrated with the Commerce Department's delay in implementing controls over the export of certain Nvidia chips to China.

Bessent said on CNBC that his department, along with the departments of State and Defense and the U.S. Trade Representative, were in favor of adding Megaspeed to an export control list for months but that the Commerce Department was in charge of the matter.

"I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s," he said. Commerce "has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes."

Bessent's comments were an unusually public rebuke of the Commerce Department, which oversees U.S. government controls over exports of sensitive, high-tech goods. The comments come as Nvidia's ties to Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which prominently touts the companies' partnership on its website, play a prominent role in the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang .

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has come under increasing scrutiny because of his reportedly close relationship with Huang. The New York Times reported Thursday that Lutnick resisted placing greater limits on the sale of Nvidia's more advanced chips to China. Chinese firms have accessed Nvidia's chips through companies like Megaspeed.

national.title: The Trump administration's voter roll crusade could continue
national.summary: Election officials are preparing for the Trump administration's pressure tactics over potential noncitizens on state voter rolls to continue, though recent court rulings pose new obstacles.
national.body:
In the weeks before Election Day, the Trump administration escalated its hunt for voter fraud and its pressure on election officials — especially in California — to crack down on illegal voting by non-U.S. citizens.

Now, with Election Day come and gone, election officials and civil rights attorneys are preparing for the administration to continue its search for noncitizens on state voter rolls, as well as what they see as intimidation tactics toward election officials.

"It's clear that there is this drive to try to conjure up facts that just don't exist. I don't think that's going to change," James Williams, county executive for California's Santa Clara County, told NPR. "So we fully are prepared to continue to deal with this."

In recent weeks, federal prosecutors announced criminal charges against dozens of people who are accused of voting or registering to vote without being a citizen. Yet compared to overall numbers of voters, noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare . And since summer, the administration has touted what turned out to be grossly inflated numbers of noncitizens on state voter rolls.

Voting Tens of millions cast ballots for midterms despite worries of Trump's interference In mid-October, federal officials alleged they had found 20,000 "likely" noncitizens on California's voter rolls. The Department of Justice sued the state to try to force election officials not to count ballots of voters whose citizenship had not been verified. A federal judge and a federal appeals court rejected the DOJ's requests , and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to intervene .

In the days leading up to Election Day, with the lawsuit pending, U.S. attorneys in California sent grand jury subpoenas to several counties, asking for records related to how local officials responded to DOJ's demands.

Though DOJ dropped its lawsuit last week, it has not rescinded these subpoenas.

"We have ongoing cases and investigations in various states surrounding voter process," U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said at a Thursday press conference. "We are actively, and will continue to investigate election integrity cases criminally and civilly, and that wasn't expected to start or stop — no matter what the results of the election were last week."

national.title: Navy has quietly fired some commanders and other officials, drawing congressional pushback
national.summary: The firings are a break from the Navy's longstanding policy to announce major removals of commanders and other highly visible officials. They also follow an increasing level of secrecy over military operations, especially in the Middle East.
national.body:
Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Navy has quietly fired or removed several top officers in recent months but broke with its usual practice of announcing those changes, drawing pushback from Congress.

Two Democratic lawmakers said Thursday that the Navy failed to inform Congress that it fired the entire leadership team of a nuclear-powered attack submarine last month after an underwater collision. Separately, the sea service in September fired the commander of a destroyer deployed to the Middle East, according to a defense official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to describe sensitive personnel matters.

Dr. Brian Monahan, a Navy rear admiral and attending physician for Congress and the Supreme Court, also departed his post during a Navy investigation — with no public announcement or confirmation.

All three are a break from the Navy's longstanding policy to announce major removals of commanders and other highly visible officials. They also follow an increasing level of secrecy over military operations, especially in the Middle East.

"As a result of the Navy's failure to communicate, what should have been a standard exercise in information sharing has instead raised questions about the Navy's commitment to transparency and its commitment to a productive working relationship with Congress," Reps. Joe Courtney of Connecticut and Adam Smith of Washington wrote in a letter to Navy leaders.

The developments could set up a contentious confirmation hearing next week for acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao as he seeks to permanently take over as the top civilian official.

In a letter to Cao and the Navy's top uniformed officer, Adm. Daryl Caudle, Courtney and Smith said they had "deep frustration" over the Navy's failure to notify the House Armed Services Committee about the firing of the commander, second in command and top enlisted sailor of the USS South Dakota submarine.

national.title: Boy found alive after 6 days lost in wilderness: "Grounded for life"
national.summary: Video shot from the rescue helicopter showed the boy was shirtless and sunburned. He was wearing shorts and boots and was using towels as blankets.
national.body: A 17-year-old boy with autism was found alive Thursday after six days lost in eastern Australian woodlands. The boy, whom police identified only as William, had begun camping with a teenage friend when he disappeared last Friday near Walhalla, a former gold-mining town 185 kilometers (115 miles) east of Melbourne, police said. A police helicopter crew found him surrounded by wilderness lying asleep on a flat rock beside a creek, and he was later reunited with his mother. William was in good spirits and mostly in good health, the police statement said. Video shot from the rescue helicopter showed he was shirtless and sunburned. He was wearing shorts and boots and was using towels as blankets. "I'm just over the moon that he's alive," his mother, Elizabeth, told reporters. The AP has decided not to provide her family name to avoid identifying her son. "And he's never leaving the house again. He's grounded for life. He's not going anywhere ever again," she joked.Police video showed Elizabeth embrace her son after the rescue helicopter landed to complete its mission. William was later taken to a hospital for his health to be monitored, police said."Amazingly, William is in good spirits and for the most part, in good health," they said in the statement.William's family have said he has Level 2 autism. That requires "substantial support," according to the Australian advocacy group Autism360. Such a person may have marked deficits in verbal and non-verbal social communication and rely heavily on routines and predictable activities. Disruption can cause significant distress. The Southern Hemisphere spring weather had been mild for the past week in the alpine region where William was lost and there had been little rain. Elizabeth had dropped off her son and his friend last Friday for a weekend of camping. William walked a short distance from the campsite to the drop-off location to collect more camping equipment but never returned to his friend, police said. After becoming lost, William trekked for days up and down "some very steep terrain," Acting Police Inspector Jason Benbow said. He spent the last two days where he was found at the creek, trapped by the steepness of his surrounds 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the his camp site, Benbow said. national.title: Alex Murdaugh wants murder indictments tossed, saying agent lied
national.summary: Alex Murdaugh's attorneys are going back to court, this time trying to get his original murder indictments dismissed.
national.body: Attorneys for Alex Murdaugh are expected in court Friday to ask a judge to throw out the original murder indictments for killing his wife and son, alleging the chief investigator in the case lied to the grand jury.Murdaugh is facing a retrial on the murder charges after the South Carolina Supreme Court threw out his convictions and life sentence, ruling that a court clerk improperly influenced jurors against him during his 2023 trial.Even if the longshot request to dismiss the indictments is granted by Judge Debra McCaslin at Friday's pretrial hearing, it may not stop or even postpone an April retrial for the disgraced lawyer. Prosecutors can seek another set of grand jury indictments as soon as next month, and defense attorneys said they won't stop them. But a ruling for Murdaugh would be another rebuke of the chief investigator, State Law Enforcement Division agent David Owen.A judge last year threw out a different murder case Owen was involved in because the dead woman's mother told the agent about a suicide threat her daughter made days before she died that Owen never relayed to prosecutors or defense attorneys.Owen abruptly retired in 2024, not long after he was honored as State Law Enforcement Officer of the Year. He has acknowledged mistakes in the Murdaugh case, but denied intentionally misleading the grand jury. Prosecutors said Murdaugh, 58, killed his wife, Maggie, and younger son, Paul, on their sprawling property in the South Carolina Lowcountry in 2021. Murdaugh is spending decades in prison for stealing millions of dollars from clients, and has admitted in court that he is a thief, insurance cheat, bad lawyer and longtime opioid addict. But he denies being a killer. Defense lawyers said that as prosecutors sought the indictments, Owen told the Colleton County grand jury that blood spatter was found on a T-shirt Murdaugh was wearing the night of the killings. An earlier report from state agents said there were no blood stains, and no such evidence was introduced at trial.Murdaugh's lawyers have repeatedly pointed out how little evidence prosecutors have. national.summary: When Democrats take over Congress in January, one of their many oversight targets will be Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., whose overhaul of longstanding vaccine guidance and cuts to medical research over the past two years have drawn fiery criticism. Some high-ranking lawmakers have suggeste
national.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — When Democrats take over Congress in January, one of their many oversight targets will be Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., whose overhaul of longstanding vaccine guidance and cuts to medical research over the past two years have drawn fiery criticism. Some high-ranking lawmakers have suggested impeaching him.

But those efforts could conflict with another growing priority for many lawmakers on the left: nurturing areas of common ground with Kennedy's Make America Healthy Again followers with the aim of securing their political support.

It could prove a difficult balance, since many MAHA activists whom Democrats are courting as part of their new coalition still view Kennedy as their closest ally.

"It's an unenviable position for Democrats to be in," said Matt Motta, a professor at Boston University School of Public Health. In addition to treading carefully not to upset MAHA voters, Motta said, the lawmakers will also have to answer to a left-leaning base that wants more accountability from Kennedy on vaccines as measles outbreaks surge around the country.

WATCH: Some MAHA backers grow frustrated with Trump's health policies

Some members of the MAHA movement said they're eager to work with Democrats to pass legislation on shared interests, like regulating pesticides and making school lunches healthier. But extensive investigations into Kennedy, or hostility toward him, could complicate those collaborations.

"I'm not saying that the Democratic leadership can't continue to have an irrational war on Secretary Kennedy until they collapse," said Mark Gorton, president of the Kennedy-aligned MAHA Institute. "But when they do that, they alienate all the MAHA voters out there, the people who really care about fighting corporate capture."

Kennedy, a lifelong Democrat before running for president as an independent in 2024 and then throwing his support behind President Donald Trump's campaign, has repeatedly clashed with his former party since joining the Trump administration.

national.title: The polar vortex just broke a new record but experts aren't sure what it means for this winter's weather
national.summary: The polar vortex has reversed direction leading to the earliest sudden stratospheric warming on record. Will this bring an early taste of winter?
national.body:
The spiralling winds of the polar vortex high above the Arctic have reversed direction marking the earliest 'major sudden stratospheric warming' on record.

These polar winds usually blow in a westerly direction keeping cold air locked high above the North Pole.

However in recent weeks the polar vortex has weakened and shifted position. Observations have now shown a switch to easterly winds, which experts say defines a 'major sudden stratospheric warming' or SSW.

Similar disruptions can occur during winter and are often linked with colder weather in the UK. But this event happening so early in autumn is unprecedented in modern observations.

The polar vortex is a normal feature of our climate in the months around winter. As the North Pole tilts away from the sun, temperatures above the Arctic drop and strong westerly winds form in the stratosphere.

Sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) is when a rapid and dramatic rise in temperature occurs high in the stratosphere, roughly 10 to 30 miles (15-50km) above Earth's surface.

It can happen due to atmospheric disturbences causing a shift in the position or shape of the polar vortex which can make its winds weaken.

This sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) can eventually lead to the strong westerlies reversing into easterly winds.

national.title: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
national.summary: The fact the question of European security now features in discussions is viewed in Moscow as a victory, BBC Russia Editor Steve Rosenberg says.
national.body:
Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.

That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.

The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."

Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.

What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.

The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 – the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.

Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.

national.title: Microsoft seeing "continued recovery" amid major worldwide outage
national.summary: A Microsoft outage involving services like Outlook and Teams has dragged on for hours and impacted many users, companies and government services
national.body: From Asia to the U.S., a Microsoft outage involving services like Outlook and Teams has dragged on into a second day, impacting users, companies and government operations around the world.The outage was affecting a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down. KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia (AP) — High airfares could become the new norm as airlines contend with soaring jet fuel prices and mounting operating costs, the Association of Asia Pacific Airlines' chief said Friday.

Wong Hong, director-general of the association grouping 18 airlines in the region, said carriers were trying to contain ticket prices while protecting their finances and avoiding fare increases that could drive passengers away.

But the industry is operating in a substantially different cost environment from a year ago when jet fuel was about $80 a barrel, compared with around $180 currently, he said. Fuel accounts for a third of airline operating costs, making further price increases a threat to carriers' financial performance, he said.

"I believe so," Wong said after an AAPA conference when asked whether high airfares would become a lasting feature rather than a temporary adjustment. "We are living in completely different market conditions and a completely different cost environment ... and it looks like these high prices will continue to prevail."

On whether airlines could implement another round of fare increases if fuel prices remain high, Wong said there was no clear answer as passenger price sensitivity varies across markets.

Major airlines across the Asia-Pacific, Europe and North America have raised base fares, hiked fuel surcharges or added extra fees since the Iran war began in late February.

The AAPA's data showed that passenger traffic across Asia-Pacific slumped for five consecutive months from April to August, before rebounding marginally in September. For the first nine months this year, overall passenger traffic in the region still grew by 1.9%.

national.title: Democratic Senate leader Schumer set to face leadership challenge
national.summary: Maryland Senator Van Hollen says "new leadership" is needed for Democrats following the party's recent midterm successes.
national.body:
US Senator Chuck Schumer is facing a challenge to his position as US Senate majority leader from his fellow Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, as the party prepares to take control of Congress after sweeping the midterm elections.

Van Hollen, 67, said in a post on X on Thursday that Americans voted for change earlier this month and "to deliver, we need new leadership".

Schumer, 75, has led Democrats in the chamber since 2017, serving as both majority and minority leader. He was first elected to the Senate in 1999.

Following the midterms earlier this month, his position has come under pressure by some left-wing Democrats who see him as too moderate and part of the party establishment.

Responding to the challenge, Schumer, who represents New York, said he welcomes "any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead".

He added that he is "proud of what we've accomplished together" in the midterms, and he has "the votes to continue as Democratic leader".

The vote on Senate leader will be held behind closed doors in early December and the winner will assume the role on 4 January, when Democrats take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives after their midterms successes.

The move by Van Hollen, who represents Maryland, marks the most significant step by a high-profile Democrat to challenge the party's existing leadership following last week's midterms victory.

Germany's foreign and domestic intelligence services are to be given greater powers to combat espionage, terrorism and sabotage after the country's parliament, the Bundestag, approved a major overhaul of its legislation.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, who championed the bill, has called it a "reform of the century", necessary because of the increasing threats from foreign powers.

But the Left Party's security spokeswoman, Clara Bünger, said Dobrindt was creating a new German secret police.

The legislation gives numerous new powers to Germany's BND federal intelligence service, and its BfV domestic service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution.

In the Bundestag, 309 MPs voted in favour of the new law on intelligence services, while 190 voted against and 71 abstained.

For historical reasons, German intelligence has mainly focused on gathering information rather than acting on it.

In future, German spies working for the BND, which is responsible for foreign intelligence, will be able to conduct covert operations abroad, including sabotage.

This could include paralysing the servers of state-sponsored hacker groups, disrupting disinformation networks, or even disrupting supply chains for weapons.

national.body:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed the Commerce Department, run by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec Nvidia chips, as the fallout from the scandal widens.

There is growing pressure on Lutnick across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions.

Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy.

Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it had been smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but is not on a list of firms that US companies are prevented from working with.

Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".

"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.

Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.

national.title: Billy Evans calls his portrayal in Elizabeth Holmes documentary "crazy"
national.summary: Billy Evans, the partner of Elizabeth Holmes, opened up about his portrayal in a hit documentary on "CBS Sunday Morning."
national.body: Billy Evans, the long-time partner of disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, opened up about his reaction to the hit documentary "You Can See Everything" during his first TV interview. "You Can See Everything," directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, follows Holmes and Evans in the weeks before she began her prison sentence for defrauding investors. Holmes claimed that she had invented technology that could run a battery of medical tests from a single drop of blood. Those claims were found to be fraudulent. Holmes is currently serving a 10-year sentence in federal prison on charges of wire fraud and conspiracy. She maintains her innocence. Evans' full interview will air on "CBS Sunday Morning" this weekend. In a preview clip, Evans told CBS News chief correspondent Matt Gutman that he loved the three-hour documentary, while also acknowledging it makes him appear "crazy," like a manipulative partner or even a villain. "I would have preferred for that not to be the case, but it's entertainment. I didn't get to control that edit," Evans said. Fans of the movie fixated on scenes where Evans appeared controlling or manipulative towards Holmes and Fielder. In one scene, Evans takes a bowl of eggs away from Holmes and claims she's not whisking them correctly. In another, he claims to know what Fielder is thinking. Later in the documentary, he reveals he has power of attorney over Holmes while she serves her sentence and controls her social media accounts. Holmes and Evans share two children. Evans said that while he disagrees with his portrayal, he thinks the documentary captures Holmes accurately. "I think my goal was to have people see Elizabeth. And when I watch that movie, I see the person that I love in exactly who she is," Evans said. Evans said that it was Holmes' advice that inspired him to share his side of the story with CBS News. "You gotta learn really painful lessons sometimes in life. And with Elizabeth going through everything she did in the press, the lesson that was ingrained in us is 'You can't lose your voice,'" Evans told Gutman. "So I look forward to speaking with you." "You Can See Everything" has become a sensation in the weeks since it was released. It has grossed over $80 million worldwide, and there is speculation that it could become the first documentary to be nominated for best picture at the Academy Awards.

national.title: Trump's Justice Department faces a new era of scrutiny under a Democratic-led Congress
national.summary: The Justice Department has functioned for nearly two years as an extension of the White House, unchecked by a Republican-controlled Congress as it pursued investigations into President Donald Trump's enemies, fired waves of career employees and defended administration stances that judges across the
national.body:
Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Justice Department has functioned for nearly two years as an extension of the White House, unchecked by a Republican-controlled Congress as it pursued investigations into President Donald Trump's enemies, fired waves of career employees and defended administration stances that judges across the country repeatedly deemed legally dubious.

Now, sweeping Democratic gains in Congress have shifted the balance of power in Washington, teeing up an onslaught of expected investigations into those actions and others as well as scrutiny from the majority party that the current Justice Department had until now managed to skirt.

The department has, at least publicly, appeared unbowed by the altered landscape.

Attorney General Todd Blanche says the department will cooperate with Congress but has also insisted that "we will not back down" from the Republican president's agenda. Meanwhile, a top aide told prosecutors on a call to prepare to be on "wartime" footing and a U.S. attorney publicly warned a top Democrat about planned congressional investigations.

It sets the stage for a pugilistic dynamic as Democrats promise to join already-skeptical courts in reining in the Trump administration while a Justice Department depleted by the losses of thousands of career employees and the postelection departures of senior leaders pledges to push ahead with its agenda.

Even though Democrats hold the gavel, they're short on foolproof ways to guarantee Republican cooperation. Lawsuits can take years, subpoenas can be arduous to enforce and criminal contempt referrals for noncompliance would be sent to the Trump administration Justice Department, where they will almost certainly not be acted on.

"It's a standoff and I don't know what the answer to that is yet," said Stan Brand, a former general counsel for the House of Representatives. "I don't know if the Congress knows."

national.body: Washington — Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10, according to a U.S. official, amid intensifying scrutiny of the Commerce Department's oversight of the export of powerful AI chips following the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.A growing number of Republicans are calling on Lutnick to answer questions about the Commerce Department's apparent delay in adding Singapore-based company Megaspeed International to the U.S. government's Entity List, which would have restricted the company's ability to get access to advanced AI chips.Megaspeed was previously led by Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy who had an affair with Jensen Huang. The U.S. government suspects Megaspeed of directing advanced Nvidia chips to China, circumventing a U.S. export ban.GOP Sen. Jim Banks of Indiana, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, told Fox News on Thursday that "we know that the Department of Commerce, Secretary Lutnick, it appears, used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur even though President Trump has directed his administration and the Department of Commerce not to allow that to happen."On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent repeatedly emphasized that the Treasury Department and other parts of the executive branch had pushed for restrictions on Megaspeed, laying the blame for the delay at the feet of the Commerce Department."Treasury, War, [the U.S. Trade Representative] and State, they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months, but Commerce has the pen," Bessent told CNBC. "And you will have to ask them about their internal processes."Bessent declined to comment on reported tensions between himself and Lutnick. The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.

national.title: Ukraine fires nearly 1,200 drones at Russia as U.S.-led talks consider wider European security
national.summary: Ukraine fired almost 1,200 drones at Russian targets overnight in one of its biggest aerial attacks since Moscow's invasion nearly five years ago.
national.body:
Samya Kullab, Associated Press Samya Kullab, Associated Press

Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press

KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukraine fired almost 1,200 drones at Russian targets overnight in one of its biggest aerial attacks since Moscow's invasion nearly five years ago.

Meanwhile, U.S. and Russian negotiators raised the stakes in talks to stop the fighting by including for discussion wider European security arrangements that have been in place since the end of the Cold War. That change, long sought by Moscow, has alarmed European leaders and placed a question mark over NATO's future role.

"Russia wants to talk about questions of European security architecture. We don't need to talk about that. There is one," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, referring to the NATO military alliance.

After two days of talks with Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi this week, U.S. envoys went in person to brief Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who was meeting with European leaders in Dublin, Ireland.

Further talks are planned as negotiators seek a breakthrough in peace efforts, according to U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also President Donald Trump's son-in-law.

Europe sees a Russian 'trap' in talks about continental security Kushner said Russia has agreed to include Europe in upcoming talks, after Moscow's long insistence that the continent's governments should be excluded because they were part of the problem by supporting Ukraine.

national.title: Van Hollen to challenge Schumer for Senate Democratic leader
national.summary: Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Thursday that he will run for Senate Majority Leader in the next Congress, setting up a challenge to Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer after the party swept to power in the midterm elections.
national.body:
Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Thursday that he will run for Senate Majority Leader in the next Congress, setting up a challenge to Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer after the party swept to power in the midterm elections.

Van Hollen said in a statement that "the American people called for change" and that is why he is running.

"It's now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership," Van Hollen said. "This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people. That is why I'm running for Senate Majority Leader."

Schumer has said he has the necessary support to win the race, which will be the first contested election for Senate Democratic leader in decades. The closed-door, secret-ballot election will be held in early December.

WATCH: Sen. Chuck Schumer speaks after Democrats win control of Senate

The question of whether to reelect Schumer has already divided the caucus and many senators have declined to say publicly how they will vote, even before Van Hollen entered the race. They have privately deliberated about what message to take from the election and many are torn — Schumer recruited many of the party's winning candidates and raised money for them, but progressive groups are pushing for his removal.

Making the pitch for his reelection, Schumer has been working with Democratic senators one-on-one to form an agenda for 2027. In private caucus meetings this week, Schumer opened discussion on a broad plan for their first 100 days in power that included healthcare and tariff legislation and efforts to stop the Iran war.

national.title: Manchester United names USMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino as its manager
national.summary: Mauricio Pochettino is out as head coach of the U.S. men's national soccer team. Pochettino led the U.S. to the round of 16 at last year's World Cup. He's departing to coach Manchester United.
national.body:
Mauricio Pochettino, who took over an ailing U.S. men's national soccer team in 2024 and led the squad to a Round of 16 finish in the 2026 World Cup, is departing to take over as coach of famed Manchester United.

Soccer Edition How coach Mauricio Pochettino made believers out of the U.S. World Cup team Pochettino was the highest-profile manager the U.S. had ever hired. His aggressive attacking style of play won praise from his players and fans alike. At the 2026 World Cup, the USMNT finished first in its group and won its first knockout-round game since 2002. Pochettino's three wins were the most at any World Cup by a USMNT coach.

As a player, he represented Argentina in the 2002 World Cup and played in soccer leagues in Spain and France. As a coach, he managed some of Europe's most recognizable clubs: Tottenham Hotspur, Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain. Last August, he signed an extension to lead the USMNT through the 2030 World Cup, giving him a full four-year cycle to build the team into a true contender.

Pochettino will lead the U.S. for two more games — against Haiti in the coming days — before departing for Manchester United.

national.title: UN watchdog 'increasingly concerned' over uninspected Iran nuclear site
national.summary: It says it has never been able to visit a uranium enrichment plant at Isfahan which Iran announced over a year ago.
national.body:
The UN's nuclear watchdog has said it is "increasingly concerned" about a nuclear facility in Iran which it has not been allowed to inspect.

Iran informed the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) of plans to set up the uranium enrichment plant in the city of Isfahan a day before Israel began attacking its nuclear sites last June. The US joined the strikes later that month.

In a report seen by news agencies, the IAEA said it does not know the exact location or whether it contains nuclear material.

Since the start of the latest war, Iran has restricted IAEA inspectors' access to its nuclear sites, preventing the agency from verifying its enriched uranium stockpile.

Under a 2015 nuclear deal, Iran agreed to limit its enriched uranium stockpile to 300kg and enrichment to 3.67% purity. It subsequently exceeded both.

Before the June 2025 strikes, it had accumulated an estimated 441kg enriched to 60%, close to weapons grade.

The nuclear complex at Isfahan suffered extensive damage in US and Israeli strikes, particularly the parts above the ground. The condition of its underground facilities is not clear.

The IAEA believes much of Iran's highly enriched uranium was stored there.

national.title: How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
national.summary: Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself.
national.body:
New York business correspondent Published 5 hours ago How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang?

The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. He had met Trump repeatedly, travelled with him to Britain and, in May, joined him on Air Force One for his trip to China.

Jensen Huang wasn't just another tech billionaire seeking the president's ear. He had become an important voice in one of the biggest arguments inside the administration: how much of America's most advanced technology should be allowed to reach China.

Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022, believing they could help Beijing develop its military and technological capabilities.

But enforcing those restrictions is difficult. Chips can be bought legally by customers in countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and then diverted to China. Chinese companies can also rent access to computing power through data centres outside the country.

Jensen Huang has long argued that the restrictions are counterproductive. They shut Nvidia out of a huge market and encourage Chinese companies to develop their own alternatives. Trump appeared sympathetic to this view, allowing Nvidia to resume sales of certain chips to China last year in return for a share of the revenue, although its most advanced Blackwell chips remain off limits.

The allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, of no relation but a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, have raised the possibility that a foreign intelligence operation was targeting not just a powerful businessman, but someone with unusually close access to the American president.

US intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But the affair has opened up a much bigger question: what did the administration in Washington know, and what did it do about it?

national.title: Happy World Kindness Day! Check out our kind photos of kindness to humans -- and cats
national.summary: Friday, November 13 is World Kindness Day. Your mission: Do something kind. Small acts of kindness definitely count!
national.body:
An animal rescuer carries a cat to safety amid severe floods that hit Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, in May 2024. Thousands of people — and animals — were affected in the wake of heavy rainfall and overflowing rivers. Tuane Fernandes/The Everyday Projects/Everyday Brasil hide caption

Kind-minded organizations from various countries came up with the idea and announced it on November 13, 1998. (And the date stuck.) The goal is kinda obvious — do something kind!

It doesn't matter if it's a modest action. One of the founding groups is the Small Kindness Movement of Japan. And no kind deed is too small to acknowledge. One year, the Japanese movement gave an award to a cabbie who pulled over to clear trash bags off the road lest they cause an accident. According to a report in the Christian Science Monitor, the cab driver humbly said it was "no big deal."

So on Friday, November 13, 2026, try a little kindness. To inspire you, we've talked to folks whose lives were changed by kindness — and asked the photojournalists of The Everyday Projects , a global network, to submit pictures that capture a kind moment. Animal lovers will be happy to see photos of kindness toward animals as well as an image of a support donkey — a reminder that animals can be kind to us humans, too.

A woman in Madagascar fixes a girl's hair — a gesture of tenderness, connection and kindness. Henitsoa RAFALIA hide caption

Erika Pozo helps her 12-year-old nephew, Josthyn Neira, with his math homework. Andres Yepez/EverydayEcuador hide caption

Back in 2004, Maymunah Yusuf Kadiri , a neuro-psychiatrist and mental health advocate in Nigeria, was a young doctor working in the emergency room at the Lagos State University Teaching hospital. One night sticks in her mind. It was chaos. There were accident victims everywhere. She recalls the blood, the cries and her own exhaustion.

"I hadn't eaten for over 12 hours, and my hands were shaking," says Kadiri, who was 28 at the time. "Then an elderly cleaner, one of those invisible heroes in hospitals, walked up to me with a small nylon bag." Inside was a biscuit and a sachet of water.

local.title: Meet Kendi, the Masai giraffe staying temporarily at Seneca Park Zoo
local.summary: He will ultimately be transferred to a Canadian facility accredited by the Association of Zoos & Aquariums.
local.body:
A new male Masai giraffe has arrived at Seneca Park Zoo, though his stay is temporary.

Kendi, a one year old male, was transferred from The Greenville Zoo in South Carolina and will ultimately be transferred to a Canadian facility accredited by the Association of Zoos & Aquariums. He's at Seneca Park Zoo for training and to be tested for contagious diseases and other health issues before he crosses the border.

Officials expect Kendi, which means "loved one" in Swahili, will immediately join the zoo's giraffe habitat.

"Kendi could be with us for as little as a year and a half," Seneca Park Zoo director Bob Lee said, "...So once his training and preparation are complete, he’ll move on to join a breeding tower (giraffe grouping) of his own."

Kendi was transferred to Seneca Park Zoo at the recommendation of the Masai giraffe Species Survival Plan for training and testing before heading to Canada, according to a news release from Monroe County. The plan recognizes Seneca Park Zoo as an expert training and holding facility for Masai giraffes.

Several Canadian zoos need male Masai giraffes, while in the United States there are more males than can be accommodated long-term, according to the county.

This story includes reporting from WXXI's All Things Considered host Beth Adams.

local.summary: Since 2024, the Buffalo Bat Habitat has made it its mission to protect our bat population. Now, a nearly $400,000 grant is making that mission a little easier.
local.body: Since 2024, the Buffalo Bat Habitat has made it its mission to protect our bat population. Now, a nearly $400,000 grant is making that mission a little easier.The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (NYSDEC) awarded the $393,942 Open Space Conservation Grant to advance permanent protection of the Ripley Bat Farm, an 84-acre property on Lake Erie.The grant will support the Buffalo Bat Habitat's larger overall mission to protect one of the region's largest little brown bat (Myotis lucifugus) maternity colonies."If you're afraid, learn about them. And after that, if you want something to be afraid of, contemplate a world without them," Founder and President Brian Caughel said. "I have 10 grandkids, and I don't want them to inherit a world without bats."The bat population once numbering nearly 2,000 individuals declined to fewer than 40 bats by 2016. One of the leading causes behind the sharp decline was the spread of White-nose Syndrome (WNS), a fungal disease that can be fatal to hibernating bats.Ripley Bat Farm is home to a colony of little brown bats that has demonstrated remarkable resilience amid the spread of WNS. During the recent monitoring season, the colony was estimated at approximately 300 to 350 little brown bats."We need to provide a place where the bats can roost from spring to fall," Caughel said.The state grant will support the acquisition of 62.8 acres of the property, including associated expenses such as legal fees, appraisals and surveys. However, the organization is still raising funds to purchase 4 acres of land. In this season of giving thanks, a local church is banding together with others around the region to break bread with their Greater Rochester neighbors.

The Harvest Time Sanctuary will host its Gathered in Gratitude dinner on Saturday, with added help from volunteers from the New Beginnings Fellowship of Churches.

Bishop Karen Horace is the senior pastor at Harvest Time Sanctuary. She says she hopes the free community meal will bring in not just those experiencing food insecurity, but also anyone who may be lonely for Thanksgiving.

"I believe that if people know that, hey, I can go over here and, on this day, I can get a good meal, and the people are loving and kind and caring. I'll do that again. And not only that, but I'll go and I'll tell somebody," said Bishop Horace.

As a member of the New Beginnings Fellowship, Bishop Horace says she hopes Harvest Time Sanctuary can go further beyond the traditional idea of community service.

"It's not enough to just have resources. We want to make an impact. We want to be able to touch somebody's life and touch somebody's heart. We want to be able to give to such the degree that the people who receive know that there's no strings attached, and the mere fact that, hey, here it is. Here, if you need it, come get it," she said.

local.title: Borinquen Dance Theatre to usher in a new era of the company
local.summary: After 45 years as the artistic director for Borinquen Dance Theatre, its founder Nydia Padilla-Rodriguez is retiring in December.
local.body:
Growing up in Rochester, dancing wasn't encouraged in his home, Bermudez said. But after getting into trouble at Monroe Middle School, staff member and mentor Sandra Martinez insisted he stay after school for a program that would change his life.

Decades later, Bermudez is preparing to take the reins of Borinquen Dance Theatre , succeeding founder Nydia Padilla-Rodriguez, who is retiring in December after 45 years as the organization's artistic director. In that time, she built an award-winning, youth-oriented program aimed at building self-confidence and discipline through dance while celebrating Puerto Rican culture.

For Bermudez, the new role represents a new chapter in a career shaped by dance, mentorship, and a commitment to helping the youth.

Bermudez was born in Puerto Rico but mainly grew up in the city of Rochester.

He described himself as an at-risk youth and was very angry at the family dynamics he experienced at home.

He said dancing wasn't considered masculine in his household. Martinez sent a letter to his parents saying he was staying after school for extra help when in reality he was joining a dance program, which Bermudez ended up loving.

"I got into some trouble and Sandra (Martinez) was the one that said, "You're going to stay after school for a program,’ and I said, ‘No, I'm not.’ She said, ‘Yes, you are.’ It was a dance program. I said, ‘No, I'm not.’” Bermudez said.

Years later, Bermudez became a part of the Movida Dance Company in Rochester, where he taught and performed as a principal dancer for 15 years. It was during his time at Movida where he was exposed to Borinquen Dance Theatre at its performances. The two companies shared a dance studio at the time.

local.summary: James Richard Morrison (Jim), age 76, passed away on November 11th, 2026 at home with his family beside him, Jim leaves behind a lifetime of memories and a family who loved him dearly. Jim was a hard worker. He spent many years on the road as an over-the-road truck driver, later driving for Hope’s W
local.body:
James Richard Morrison (Jim), age 76, passed away on November 11th, 2026 at home with his family beside him, Jim leaves behind a lifetime of memories and a family who loved him dearly.

Jim was a hard worker. He spent many years on the road as an over-the-road truck driver, later driving for Hope's Windows, and eventually working for Lakeshore Septic. Jim was never one to sit idle. There was always something to do, something to fix, or someone to share a joke with. He always had a story to tell and was quick with his famous Dad-joke wit.

For many years, Jim enjoyed hunting and fishing, a love he happily passed along to his children and grandchildren. He found enjoyment in the simple things: tinkering in the garage, collecting his John Deere tractors, puttering with his apple press, and working with his honey bees. Sitting on the front porch relaxing, or just enjoying time with his devoted dog Macie, who never left his side. He also enjoyed sharing his knowledge with anyone willing to spend a little time with him. Jim was always ready to teach someone something new. Like building Butterfly houses.

Jim knew the value of a dollar and made sure to pass that lesson along to his children. He believed in hard work and solid values. Whether it was pulling nails to recycle or saving things to repurpose, Jim never believed in letting anything go to waste. He could find a use for just about anything. But while he was careful with a dollar, he was never cheap when it came to the people he loved. He made sure his family never went without, and if he knew someone was in need, Jim would be the first to lend a hand, helping however he could and giving the shirt off his back if necessary. That was just the kind of man he was.

But above all, Jim's greatest joy was his family. He treasured the everyday moments and the life he built with his wife. He was a devoted husband of almost 52 years to his cherished wife, Priscilla (Frazier). Her "Jimmy" was the love of her life. You rarely saw one without the other.

He was a loving father to his daughter, Stephanie (Steven) Horner of Cherry Creek, and his son, James (Cassandra) Morrison of Randolph. He was a proud and loving grandfather to his four grandsons, Ethan (Bubba), Finnley, Grayson, and Henry, who meant the world to him. Being a Grandpa changed Jim, his kids often joked how much the grandkids got away with what "we never would have!" He truly loved his boys and sharing his knowledge of things with them.

local.title: Fredonia eyes bond note for water project
local.summary: Three Fredonia trustees devoted their board meeting reports this week to the water system saga. Most notably, Trustee Tim Mulholland said the village is eyeing a bond anticipation note to help fund its North County Water District connection project. Mulholland described a meeting about financing opt
local.body:
Three Fredonia trustees devoted their board meeting reports this week to the water system saga.

Most notably, Trustee Tim Mulholland said the village is eyeing a bond anticipation note to help fund its North County Water District connection project.

Mulholland described a meeting about financing options for the project. Financial consultant Rick Ganci, Trustee LeeAnn Lazarony, and Treasurer Erlyssa LeBsau joined him in the meeting.

The Fredonia officials gave Ganci a "financial snapshot of our village. One of the immediate priorities is reimbursing our village’s water fund for approximately $500,000 in engineering and related project expenses already incurred before our recent pause."

Mulholland continued, "We discussed whether it would make more sense to pursue financing for the entire project, or focus initially on reimbursing the water fund. Given that the project’s ultimate financing needs are still being determined, that we anticipate potential grant funding, and we aren't ready to move forward with this project during this pause, the appropriate approach appears to be to pay back our water fund as an appropriate first step, and Ganci agreed."

LeBeau consulted with Ganci to confirm that a September resolution provides sufficient authorization to do a bond anticipation note, Mulholland said. "This short term borrowing mechanism will allow us to reimburse the water fund for those expenses already paid," he said.

Ganci wants to have the note ready by December, and "also offered to have his team review the project’s finances, and other potential funding opportunities and grants that may be available to us," Mulholland added.

"While municipalities our size have limited options, it is worth exploring opportunities to strengthen our finances without unnecessarily burdening our taxpayers. That's very important to all of us, and myself, especially," he concluded.

local.title: Are Democrats serious about affordability?
local.summary: Emboldened by the scale of Democratic victories in the midterms, a small group of liberals is trying to blow up a carefully negotiated bipartisan agreement that would make it easier to build in America. Failure to pass this compromise during the lame-duck session would send a loud message that the i
local.body:
Emboldened by the scale of Democratic victories in the midterms, a small group of liberals is trying to blow up a carefully negotiated bipartisan agreement that would make it easier to build in America. Failure to pass this compromise during the lame-duck session would send a loud message that the incoming Democratic majorities aren't as serious about affordability as candidates said they were on the stump. And a deal this good for the economy is unlikely to materialize in the next Congress, which is why unions for the building trades and electricians are fighting to get it done.

Unfortunately, Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York), the presumptive next House speaker, wants to reopen negotiations. His spokesperson said on Thursday that the deal "falls short in several areas." Without expressing opposition, Jeffries's office said: "We must once again support the clean energy economy and combat the climate crisis with the fierce urgency of now."

Except the deal on the table is great for the environment. Democratic negotiators in the Senate consulted closely with their House counterparts. The agreement would make it much easier to build clean energy projects and the transmission lines needed to connect them to the grid. While some environmental groups criticize the compromise for reducing regulatory barriers to construct fossil fuel infrastructure, a recent analysis by the independent Rhodium Group concluded that the legislation would probably cut carbon emissions overall.

Given the soaring demand for energy, the reforms are necessary to boost production capacity and thereby lower electricity prices for Americans. The Rhodium analysis projects that if the bill passes, the average household would see its electricity bills drop $50 to $78 a year by 2040. The legislation also includes a provision obligating states to require large energy consumers, such as data centers, to pay for their electricity use.

Unfortunately, there is a potent "degrowth" faction inside the environmental movement for whom no deal would ever be good enough. These activists don't want to create enough supply to meet energy needs. They want to make it harder to build, in the hope that scarcity will force society to reduce consumption. Down that path lies national stagnation.

Other Democrats may want an agreement but see an opening to maximize leverage. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-California), poised to lead the House committee that oversees permitting reform, has argued for weeks that Democrats should hold out until next year to negotiate more favorable terms.

local.title: Longtime Steelers assistant coach Dick Hoak dies at 86
local.summary: PITTSBURGH (AP) — Dick Hoak, who spent more than 45 years with the Pittsburgh Steelers as a player and then an assistant coach, winning five Super Bowl rings along the way, has died. He was 86. The team announced Hoak’s death on Wednesday. No cause of death was given. “Dick represented everything th
local.body:
PITTSBURGH (AP) -- Dick Hoak, who spent more than 45 years with the Pittsburgh Steelers as a player and then an assistant coach, winning five Super Bowl rings along the way, has died. He was 86.

The team announced Hoak’s death on Wednesday. No cause of death was given.

“Dick represented everything the Steelers stand for with his toughness, loyalty, dedication and an unwavering commitment to the team,” team president Art Rooney II said in a statement.

Selected by the Steelers in the seventh round of the 1961 NFL draft after a standout career at Penn State, Hoak ran for 3,965 yards and 25 touchdowns in 10 seasons in Pittsburgh’s backfield, leading the then-struggling club in rushing three times.

Hoak, a Pro Bowler in 1968 after running for a career-best 858 yards, retired after the 1970 season and joined coach Chuck Noll’s staff as running backs coach in 1972.

Over the next three-plus decades, he served as an important touchstone and mentor for future Hall of Famers like Franco Harris and Jerome Bettis as the Steelers evolved from also-rans to one of the league’s marquee franchises.

Many of those Super Bowl-winning teams were powered by the running game that Hoak helped mold. He was so influential and important to the organization that he spanned the tenure of a pair of Hall of Fame coaches in Noll and his successor, Bill Cowher.

Cowher retained Hoak on his staff after replacing Noll in 1992 and credited Hoak for helping him shoulder the difficult task of replacing an icon.

local.body:
ASHVILLE -- A final informational forum for the Clymer, Sherman and Panama school district communities is set for the end of this month, giving residents one more chance to ask questions and get more information before the final statutory vote is scheduled.

The meeting is set to take place at 6:30 p.m. at the Ashville Hewes BOCES on November 30. The meeting is open to all community members and will be recorded and uploaded to the CSPHub website for anyone unable to attend.

"We will highlight the final recommendations from the independent feasibility study," CSP Merger Study Project Coordinator, Shelly O'Boyle, said. "Additionally, White and Partners will present updated financial data. A major focus of the format is giving residents a dedicated platform to ask questions and discuss the findings."

The town hall is the final public forum before the formal statutory vote, which is the vote that officially decides if the three districts will merge. O'Boyle said the vote has been scheduled by the New York State Commissioner of Education.

The official date for the statutory vote is December 15 from 12 p.m. to 8 p.m. Absentee ballots will be available starting on November 12.

"Voting will take place locally at each individual school district," O'Boyle said. "Residents will be able to obtain absentee and early mail ballots from their respective District Clerks. Military voters should request an early mail ballot. Proof of residency should be brought to the voting site."

The full merger feasibility study, past meetings, and more information on the CSP merger can be found at CSPHub.org.

local.summary: Pete Crow-Armstrong won the NL MVP award unanimously on Thursday after the center fielder starred for the Chicago Cubs in a majestic all-around season. Crow-Armstrong joined Houston Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez as first-time MVPs. Alvarez was the unanimous AL winner after making a run at the Triple
local.body:
Pete Crow-Armstrong won the NL MVP award unanimously on Thursday after the center fielder starred for the Chicago Cubs in a majestic all-around season.

Crow-Armstrong joined Houston Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez as first-time MVPs. Alvarez was the unanimous AL winner after making a run at the Triple Crown, hitting a career-high .316 with 42 homers and 106 RBIs for the AL West champions.

Crow-Armstrong set career highs by batting .280 with 45 homers, 107 RBIs and 41 steals in 162 games. He tied Kyle Schwarber for the major league lead in home runs, and he led the NL in runs (119), slugging percentage (.570) and OPS (.942).

He also was one of the majors’ premier defensive players. The Southern California native won his second Gold Glove, and he led the majors with 26 Outs Above Average and 23 Runs Prevented, according to Baseball Savant.

“You spend your whole life in baseball and you just don’t see this happen on a baseball field,” Cubs manager Craig Counsell said after Crow-Armstrong homered twice in an 8-4 win over Atlanta on Sept. 16. “You’re grateful to be a part of it. You’re grateful to see things like this and then you’re grateful that the fans get to see a season like this.”

Crow-Armstrong received all 30 first-place votes in balloting from the Baseball Writers’ Association of America. Four-time MVP Shohei Ohtani of the Los Angeles Dodgers finished second, and Milwaukee Brewers second baseman Brice Turang was third.

Alvarez led the majors in batting average and finished in a tie for second in the AL in homers and second by himself in RBIs, trailing Pete Alonso’s 43 homers and 113 RBIs for Baltimore.

Alvarez was Houston’s primary designated hitter, but his offensive brilliance was enough to overcome his limited contributions on defense. The four-time All-Star also led the majors in walks (109), on-base percentage (.432) and slugging percentage (.601).

The Bears senior guard completed her celebratory signing letter Thursday afternoon to atte
local.body:
Playing high-level college basketball has always been a dream for Jadyn Trocki.

When the closest Division I program to her Frewsburg home came calling a couple of years ago, it felt like the perfect situation.

The Bears senior guard completed her celebratory signing letter Thursday afternoon to attend St. Bonaventure University and play basketball for the Bonnies beginning next fall.

"Division I has always been the dream, but some DIIs were also in the equation as well," Trocki said Wednesday afternoon. "I wasn't always set on DI. I was always going to choose where I fit best."

Trocki has put together the best individual career in Frewsburg history and with it the Bears have also experienced high levels of success as a team. She is already Frewsburg's all-time leading scorer with 1,796 points and has been named the New York State Sportswriters Association's Class C Player of the Year in back-to-back seasons.

"A lot of people focus on the skill side of things, but I remember on jayvee she would get really emotional, so for me the fun part has been seeing her mental maturity. Even from the beginning of last season to the end, or during her sophomore year, she would go into a shell," Frewsburg head coach Sierra Beaver said Wednesday. "Last year, I think one of the first things I noticed at North Tonawanda was that things weren't going well in the first half and I remember at halftime, telling Sandy (Ruhlman, Jadyn's mother) we'll see how the season goes based on this second half. If Jadyn goes into a shell we're in trouble, but if she shows maturity, we're going to have a fun season. In the second half she had one of her best games."

Trocki has started every year since eighth grade after being called up to the varsity team for a postseason run at the end of her seventh-grade year.

"Around seventh grade I started taking it more seriously," Trocki said. "I started playing for bigger programs, playing throughout Pittsburgh and Erie. ... It's the one thing I really love."

entertainment.title: Valerie June Releases Uplifting Cover of Louis Armstrong’s ‘What a Wonderful World’
entertainment.summary: “Progress happens when everyday people believe in one another, come together, and work toward a more just, compassionate, and beautiful world,” she says
entertainment.body:
Valerie June has released an uplifting cover of Louis Armstrong’s “What a Wonderful World.” The single follows the release of her Brighter Blue EP, which arrived in September via Concord.

In the accompanying visual to the songwriter and multi-instrumentalist’s rendition of the song, she performs in a space decorated with white flowers, her hair adorned with decorative butterflies. The joy she expresses is contagious as she smiles while delivering the resonant lines over pedal steel accompaniment. It’s clear she relishes each line, as she dances around while playing banjo and brings both empowerment and reflection as she sings.

The feel-good, hopeful vibes are welcome in these times, and deciding to cover this song right now was an intentional, uplifting choice, as June explained in a statement. It was inspired by working with the American Revival program.

“Working with elementary and middle school students through Yo-Yo Ma and Nicholas Ma’s American Revival program gives me hope for a more beautiful world,” she said in a statement. “Many of these young people have been deeply affected by the disruption of families and communities along the border, violence in their neighborhoods, and countless other challenges. Art and music can be powerful healers. They create space for connection, expression, joy, and hope.”

entertainment.title: Inside the New Magazine About Psychedelics — And the Goddess
entertainment.summary: Thunder Perfect Mind , from longtime Rolling Stone contributor Cassady Rosenblum, explores the spiritual world all around us
entertainment.body:
The Goddess came to Cassady Rosenblum “gorgeous, and terrifying, like a multiheaded dragon who could birth a planet or destroy a galaxy, simply by licking her numerous lips.” It was 2022, and Rosenblum was in Utah reporting a story for Rolling Stone about a group of Mormons who had left the Church of Latter-Day Saints and were using psilocybin as a sacrament. As an embedded journalist, Rosenblum joined an all-women’s mushroom ceremony. In the visions that came to her that evening, she saw a “lush, benevolent, intricate universe, one woven entirely of sacredness.”

The Mother of All Creation showed her three things. “First, it was babies being born,” Rosenblum tells me. “Like all babies, throughout all time.” Then, it was seeds sprouting and plants growing, followed by rivers and waterfalls, “and I was made to understand that she is the dynamic energy that animates the universe.”

Rosenblum says she had two realizations with these visions. “One was, ‘This is who the patriarchy has been afraid of this whole time,’ and I felt for the first time that I, as a woman, was batting on the stronger team.” Four years later, she considers herself “a small part of a several-millennia baton pass” as the founder and editor-in-chief of Thunder Perfect Mind , a new print publication dedicated to the Great Mother.

The magazine’s manifesto describes itself as being “devoted to the Goddess… [by which] we do not mean a deity so much as the intelligent, pulsing power of life itself.” It calls for greater ecological awareness as Silicon Valley bets big on AI and data centers in spite of massive public pushback . It recognizes feminine rage, as women openly discuss the life-altering experience of perimenopause and menopause that generations of our foremothers dealt with in near-silence. It calls us back to our ancestors with reverence for “the sacred feminine — the portal through which all life enters and is reabsorbed,” as Rosenblum writes in her editor’s note. And for the lady, perhaps a collective awakening? Animism — the concept that non-human organisms, landforms, natural phenomena, and inanimate objects possess a spiritual essence or consciousness — is shifting from a marginalized worldview into mainstream discourse. Psychedelics are no longer considered taboo as millions of Americans are using them for the first time. The time seems ripe for “ the return of the Goddess .” Thunder Perfect Mind reflects this stirring through a curated assemblage of art, essays, and interviews. Rosenblum, a longtime Rolling Stone contributor, traces the beginnings of her “magazine-shaped altar” to that 2022 assignment in Utah. Before the mushroom ceremony, she was a self-described atheist. “I thought spirituality was really for weak-minded people,” she admits, “and it was all a Santa Claus bedtime story.” Post-ceremony, her life “swerved,” as she puts it.

entertainment.title: Heartbroken ‘General Hospital’ star reveals her husband has died after ‘sudden’ illness: ‘We were supposed to have more time’
entertainment.summary: The "One Life to Live" actress paid tribute to animator Michael John Roberts in an Instagram post, alongside a heartfelt statement on his obituary page.
entertainment.body:
Soap opera star Bree Williamson, who starred in “ General Hospital ” and “ One Life to Live ,” has announced the heartbreaking death of her husband, Michael John Roberts.

In an official obituary , Williamson and the family of her late husband revealed that the “BoJack Horseman” animator and director died at their Los Angeles home on Wednesday, after a brief battle with glioblastoma.

“We were supposed to have more time. More conversations over a good cup of coffee. More spirited debates about matters both profound and wonderfully insignificant,” the statement began.

“More laughter, more stories, more music and more ordinary moments that would someday become extraordinary memories.”

The family statement noted that the artist’s illness “came suddenly” and that the “time that followed was heartbreakingly short.”

Per the Mayo Clinic, glioblastoma is an aggressive type of brain cancer that starts in cells called astrocytes, which support nerve cells. It’s the most common malignant brain tumor in adults and makes up about half of all malignant brain tumors in adults.

In an Instagram post on Thursday, Williamson wrote, “Thank you to everyone that has reached out. We are heartbroken and taking some time.”

I’m excited to see her lead our global marketing team into this next chapter.”

Shah added, “TuneCore has always been a space for artists to distribute their music, but we know their journey begins long before that moment and continues far beyond it. I’m so excited to step into this role at a time when supporting that journey means more than ever, and look forward to leading our Global Marketing team as we build a brand that not only serves as an intrinsic part of the artists’ creative community, but also helps them succeed on their own terms.” — Ariel King
