sports.title: Failed Daiyan Henley trade exposes a flaw in the NFL's trade deadline
sports.summary: The trade deadline is the trade deadline.
sports.body:
The strange situation involving the failed trade of Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley to the Broncos reveals a major flaw in the NFL’s deadline-day machinery.

Adam Schefter of ESPN has provided the details (which we have confirmed to be accurate) in the most nonchalant, innocuous terms possible: “It is not uncommon for one team to have some medical concerns about a player while another does not. In this case, Denver had concerns about Henley following his physical. Even then, the Broncos still wanted Henley with Denver and LA discussing revised trade alternatives throughout the day, taking into account those concerns. In the end, no agreement was reached. The deal was off.”

Here’s what it means. The Chargers and Broncos struck a deal for Henley and independently communicated the terms to the NFL before the trade deadline of 4:00 p.m. ET on Tuesday, November 10. Like all trades, the Henley deal was subject to the player passing a physical.

The Broncos discovered an issue with Henley’s knee. It has, we’re told, arthritis. (As one source with neither the Chargers nor the Broncos told PFT, most if not all starting linebackers in the NFL have some degree of arthritis in their knees.)

The NFL allows trade terms to be revised after the deadline, to an extent. Per a league spokesperson: “We would permit them to change the pick compensation. They would not be able to add a player or trade a different player.”

Instead of concluding that the physical had been failed and canceling the deal (like the Ravens did with the trade for Raiders defensive end Maxx Crosby in March), the Broncos were willing to proceed with revised terms. In other words, for something less than a fourth-round pick in 2027 and a fifth-round pick in 2028, they’d still do the deal.

That’s not how it should work after the deadline. The window has closed. The deals are done, or they’re not. After 4:00 p.m. ET on November 10, the only question left to answer is whether the player passes or fails the physical.

As one source explained it, deadline-day deals have gone through in the past with terms that were revised after the deadline.

Head coach Aaron Glenn, defensive coordinator Brian Duker and offensive coordinator Frank Reich all have some history with Buffalo. sports.body: The Buffalo Bills have a new safety — Amani Hooker. You may have heard. And if you’re wondering how he’ll be deployed in Jim Leonhard’s defense, this article has you covered. Up front, Hooker is at his best in a deep-coverage role. Of course, in the modern NFL, he’s played everywhere in the back seven. But the film and numbers suggest he’s the most impactful when he can process route concepts, check the quarterback, and range to the football. On 1,172 snaps across the 2020 and 2021 campaigns — his second and third in the NFL — Hooker played 717 snaps as a free safety (61.1%) and rewarded the Titans with a total of five interceptions and 12 pass breakups in 28 games. In those years, Hooker averaged just under 42 snaps per contest. In 2024, when Hooker had five interceptions, he aligned at free safety on 55.9% of his snaps. On this note, here’s how Cole Bishop and Hooker compare in snaps by specific position to date in their NFL careers. [Image: https://platform.buffalorumblings.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/51/2026/11/Amani-Hooker-vs.-Cole-Bishop-_-Career-positional-alignment.png?quality=90&strip=all] Now I think it’s easy to see “free safety” vs. “box” labels and instantly view the difference in safety positioning through the lens of a single-high look. That’s not necessarily the case with those labels. All “free safety” means is that the defender is aligned at a deep safety spot on the field even in a split-field, two-safety look. So both safeties on a specific play can be in a “free safety” spot, an occurrence that happens frequently in the NFL. However, that graphic shows a pretty discernible difference between Hooker and Bishop’s usage in Buffalo and Tennessee respectively to date. Hooker holds a slight edge in free safety snaps, has less frequently been deployed in the box while spending a higher percentage in the slot. And Hooker’s pre-draft workout in 2019 speaks to what has been a more “coverage-based” utilization in his NFL career. sports.body: The Buffalo Bills made one move before the trade deadline, a reasonable transaction with the Tennessee Titans to acquire safety Amani Hooker. The move has been widely regarded as a wise one by the Bills. Needing help on a defense that seems destined to eventually cost Buffalo a game, pretty much everyone is of the belief that Hooker will help cover up some flaws with solid defensive back play. Well I have one thing to say to that… Yeah, pretty much. This is a case of everyone being right. I’ll give you my thoughts on the matter with a short highlight reel but this was a great move by Buffalo. Some film and opinions [Media: https://twitter.com/Kuebiko_Kami/status/2120731699164139571?a=wdetkgsxvccD9wqT5yw&s=20] What you have there for the video is Amani Hooker’s five interceptions this year. Does that seem like a lot of interceptions in what amounts to half a season? Because it is. Hooker is tied with Green Bay’s Xavier Mckinney for the lead league with that five. In reality though, Hooker should be considered the interception leader so far in 2026. McKinney’s five interceptions come from nine games, and if you like granular assessment he’s played on 604 snaps. That means he has one interception every 121-ish plays. Hooker was out for one game with a concussion and Tennessee was on their bye this week. He’s appeared in just 495 snaps, for an interception rate of one every 99 plays. In the film above, I went with just the interceptions primarily because they’re fun, but there’s plenty to see on them as well. Hooker’s anticipation and ability to read the quarterback is excellent. Over his career that’s led to variable interception totals and being transparent here, 2026 has already tied his career high, achieved in 2024. So really, the ballhawk thing is hopefully a “from now on” kinda deal. I don’t mean to suggest he’s been poor at it, only that this year is very good even for Hooker. The traits that have led to it in 2026 are good signs for all facets of safety play though. Hooker is a heads up defensive back that processes the game with speed and gets into the mix quickly. That’s been interceptions this year, but it also means he’s there for tackles and other support. I don’t want to oversell him either. sports.body: Nothing happens in a vacuum. Using words like “good” or “bad” inevitably unlocks a more nuanced “good relative to what” or “bad relative to what” conversation. Thus, when the time comes to evaluate the Buffalo Bills’ acquisition of safety Amani Hooker from the Tennessee Titans, the question of whether or not the move is good is a very different question than whether or not the move is optimal. “Good” is a value in vs. value out proposition, with the acknowledgement that the concept of value is subjective based upon how someone weights Hooker’s skill, short vs. long term considerations, and financial items. “Optimal” is instead a reflection of the level of “good” achieved from this maneuver compared to the level of “good” that could have hypothetically been achieved through a different maneuver entirely. It’s a question that folds in opportunity cost amongst all potential other maneuvers. In this author’s opinion, the Hooker transaction is both good and optimal. Other content pieces can discuss the “good” part of that statement. Hooker’s skill set, the compensation, the need at safety, the fact that he’s under contract through 2028 with reasonable cap hits…I’ll let other articles and podcasts outline why those factors all come together to form a conclusion that the addition of Hooker is a good one. I’d instead like to make the argument here that not only was the Hooker addition good, it was the most good the team could have done with its resources at the trade deadline and therefore optimal. In order to do that, I will need to discuss two separate items: what the Bills could have spent and what they could have received. Everything in life is a value proposition: what you give vs. what you get. In order to prove that the Hooker trade was optimal, I need to create a clear picture of all the potential combinations of “give” and “get” and when none of them create a better (“more good”) outcome when compared to the Hooker trade, I can then argue that the transaction was optimal. sports.title: Daniel Jones is "not happy" with Colts' roster purge
sports.summary: The Colts had a mini-fire sale in recent weeks, trading away four starters for future assets.
sports.body:
Quarterback Daniel Jones, not surprisingly, isn’t thrilled by the decision to send guard Quenton Nelson, defensive tackle DeForest Buckner, receiver Keenan Allen, and receiver Josh Downs to other teams.

“I mean, honestly, you’re not you’re not happy to see it, right? ” Jones said. “You’re a player and you’re going out there competing and doing everything you can to win games. So you’re not happy to see a lot of those decisions, and — but like I said, it’s outside of our control, and our job is to play, be prepared, and play well. So, like I said, we got a lot of trust in the guys coming in to those spots, and we’ll be ready to go.”

It’s a bad situation for the players who remain, since it will be harder for them to win with backups thrust into the lineup. But that’s how it works whenever a non-contender admits its situation and trades players.

Those who remain have to keep going, trying to win games even if they get the impression that the front office doesn’t really care.

And even though the Jets hold the Colts’ first-round pick, a bad season for Indianapolis will result in a higher spot in every round. As the Colts embark on a rebuild, it’s not crazy to think the front office hopes to sink as low in the standings as possible, since that will enhance the priority of the picks they have.

The Jets will welcome that, since they have the Colts’ first-round pick. Thanks to the failed trade for cornerback Sauce Gardner.

sports.body: The Jets recently signed former Steelers defensive lineman Isaiahh Loudermilk to their practice squad. Today, we break him down in detail. The 29-year old Loudermilk is listed at 6’7” and 293 pounds and was a fifth round pick out of Wisconsin in 2021. He has started seven games in his NFL career, with 63 tackles, six passes defensed and one sack. Background Loudermilk was a three-star high school recruit despite only having played 8-man football in a small town. He ended up going to Wisconsin, where he redshirted his first season in 2016, but then became a useful player over the next few years. In 2017, Loudermilk had six tackles in 11 games in a reserve role, adding 1.5 sacks and a pass defensed. He started the first six games of his career in 2018 and ended up with 15 tackles, 2.5 tackles for loss, three passes defensed and a sack in nine games. In 2019, he started all 14 games and had his most productive season with 24 tackles, five tackles for loss, three sacks, five pass breakups and two forced fumbles. However, Loudermilk got all Big-10 recognition for the only time in his final season as he was named as a third-teamer by the media and an honorable mention by the coaches. In just six games during the pandemic-shortened 2020 season, he had 13 tackles and two sacks. After not being invited to the scouting combine, Loudermilk played in the East-West Shrine Bowl and was eventually drafted by the Steelers in the fifth round of the 2021 draft. As a rookie, he started two games and ended up with 23 tackles, a sack and two pass breakups in 15 appearances. In 2022, Loudermilk started three times but had just seven tackles and a tackle for loss in 11 games overall. He played in 16 games in both 2023 and 2024 but did not start a game during that time. He ended up with 33 tackles, three passes defensed and a quarterback hit over the two seasons. 2025 saw Loudermilk start the first two games, although he didn’t generate any statistics. An injury in the second game sidelined him for the rest of the season. He was almost ready to return for the postseason but wasn’t cleared in time. Loudermilk signed for the Vikings in the offseason but failed to make their roster and was eventually added to the Jets’ practice squad last month.
